mainTopic: Comparing the categories of damage (שור, אש, בור) and their missing stringencies, and the משנה's rule about one who makes possible part of the damage.
overview: This amud finishes a ברייתא that compares the main categories of damage, showing that שור and אש, and then בור and אש, are each stricter than the other in some way. The גמרא then asks why the ברייתא did not also say that a שור pays for broken כלים while a בור does not. One answer says the ברייתא follows רבי יהודה, who holds a בור liable for כלים. That fails because of the ברייתא's own fire clause, which the גמרא first reads as being about כלים. The גמרא gives two ways out. Either the ברייתא follows the רבנן and simply left some cases out (תנא ושייר), or 'something not fit for fire' means scorching a field, which fits רבי יהודה. רב אשי then challenges the רבי יהודה reading, and the attempt to defend it is rejected. Next the גמרא turns to the משנה's line about making possible part of the damage. A ברייתא explains it with a pit dug to nine טפחים and finished to ten, and רב פפא shows this fits even רבי's view. Finally, רבי זירא and רב ששת suggest other examples, the five guards and adding wood to a fire. The גמרא rejects the first, and its look at the second continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Ox and fire each have a stricter side
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא announces that it will compare שור and אש, and that each has a way it is stricter than the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a way the ox is stricter than fire, and a way fire is stricter than the ox.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The ברייתא names the two categories it is about to compare, and the next two steps fill in the details.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא promises a two-sided comparison. It is not saying one category is simply worse. It is saying each has its own strict points, which it will now list one side at a time.

keyTerms.meaning: A stringency, a way something is stricter
Ox, the category of damage done by an animal
Fire, the category of damage done by a fire one is responsible for

steps.confusionAlert: Read the word order carefully. חומר בשור מבאש means 'a stringency in the ox compared to fire', so the ox is the stricter one in that phrase.

phrases.english: A stringency in Ox over Fire,
a stringency in Fire over Ox.

steps.triggerLanguage: חוֹמֶר בְּשׁוֹר מִבְּאֵשׁ, חוֹמֶר בְּאֵשׁ מִבְּשׁוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא's series of comparisons between the categories of damage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שור and אש each have a feature that makes them stricter than the other.

steps.title: How the ox is stricter than fire
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא lists four ways שור is stricter: כופר, thirty for an עבד, being forbidden for benefit after the verdict, and liability even after handing it to a חרש שוטה וקטן.
steps.simpleTranslation: How is the ox stricter than fire? If an ox kills a person, the owner pays a ransom. If it kills a slave, the owner must pay thirty. Once the ox has been sentenced, no one may benefit from it. If the owner hands it over to a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, or a minor, he is still liable. None of this applies to fire.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא fills in the first half of the comparison. It gives four laws that apply to an ox and not to fire.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Three of these laws come from the case of an ox that kills a person: כופר, thirty for an עבד, and the ox being forbidden for benefit once it is sentenced. Fire has no such laws. The fourth law is that the owner stays liable even if he handed his ox to people who are not responsible (חרש שוטה וקטן). With fire, handing it to such people does not leave the owner liable in the same way.

keyTerms.meaning: Ransom money the owner pays when his ox kills a person
The thirty (shekels) paid when an ox kills a slave
His verdict is finished, meaning the court has sentenced the ox
Forbidden to get any benefit from it
A deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, and a minor: people not legally responsible

phrases.english: The stringency in Ox over Fire:
that for the ox, one pays a ransom,
phrases.notes: שמות 21:30. This is when the ox kills a person.

phrases.english: and he is liable for the thirty of a slave,
phrases.notes: שמות 21:32. That is thirty shekels when the ox kills a slave.

phrases.english: once its verdict is finished, it is forbidden for benefit,
if he handed it to a deaf-mute, an incompetent, or a minor, he is liable;
which is not so with fire.

steps.triggerLanguage: חוֹמֶר בְּשׁוֹר מִבְּאֵשׁ – שֶׁהַשּׁוֹר מְשַׁלֵּם כּוֹפֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first half of the heading from Step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שור carries כופר, thirty for an עבד, a ban on benefit after the verdict, and liability even after handing it to a חרש שוטה וקטן. אש has none of these.

steps.title: How fire is stricter than the ox
steps.stepSummary: אש counts as מועד from the very start, while a שור does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: How is fire stricter than the ox? Fire counts as 'forewarned' from the very beginning, which is not true of an ox.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא fills in the second half of the comparison. It gives the one way fire is stricter than an ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ox that gores starts out as a תם, so the owner pays only part of the damage until it becomes known as a gorer. Fire is treated as מועד right away, because spreading and burning is simply what fire does. That means full payment from the very first damage.

keyTerms.meaning: Forewarned, meaning known to damage, so the owner pays in full
From its beginning

phrases.english: The stringency in Fire over Ox:
that fire is forewarned from its beginning,
phrases.notes: An ox that gores is 'forewarned' only after it has gored a few times. Before that it pays only part of the damage.

phrases.english: which is not so with an ox.

steps.triggerLanguage: חוֹמֶר בְּאֵשׁ מִבְּשׁוֹר – שֶׁהָאֵשׁ מוּעֶדֶת מִתְּחִילָּתָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the two-sided comparison begun in Step 1, after Step 2 gave the ox's side.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אש is מועד from the start, while שור is not.
steps.whatToRemember: שור is stricter in its special laws (כופר, thirty for an עבד, the ban on benefit, and staying liable after handing it to a חרש שוטה וקטן). אש is stricter because it is מועד from the first moment.

steps.title: Fire and pit each have a stricter side
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא moves to its next pair: אש compared with בור.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a way fire is stricter than a pit, and a way a pit is stricter than fire.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a new setup line. The ברייתא names its next pair, fire and pit, and the next two steps give the details.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same two-sided pattern repeats with a new pair. Notice that the ברייתא explains these in reverse order. It names fire first here, but in the next step it starts by explaining how the pit is stricter.

keyTerms.meaning: Pit, the category of damage done by a hole or obstacle someone created

phrases.english: A stringency in Fire over Pit,
and a stringency in Pit over Fire.

steps.triggerLanguage: חוֹמֶר בְּאֵשׁ מִבְּבוֹר, וְחוֹמֶר בְּבוֹר מִבְּאֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the ox-and-fire comparison to a new pair, fire and pit.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אש and בור each have a feature that makes them stricter than the other.

steps.title: How the pit is stricter than fire
steps.stepSummary: A בור is made from the start in a way that leads to damage, and the owner stays liable even after handing it over to a חרש שוטה וקטן.
steps.simpleTranslation: How is a pit stricter than fire? From the moment it is made, it is set up for damage. If one hands it over to a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, or a minor, one is still liable. This is not so with fire.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא explains the first half of the fire-and-pit pair: two ways a pit is stricter than fire.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Digging a pit in a place where it can cause harm makes it a source of damage from the very start. A fire, by contrast, is usually lit for a useful purpose. Also, as with an ox, handing a pit over to people who are not responsible does not free the owner from liability, while with fire the law is different.

keyTerms.meaning: The beginning of its making, meaning when it is first dug
For damage, set up to cause harm

phrases.english: The stringency in Pit over Fire:
that the beginning of its making is for damage,
if he handed it to a deaf-mute, an incompetent, or a minor, he is liable;
which is not so with fire.

steps.triggerLanguage: חוֹמֶר בְּבוֹר מִבְּאֵשׁ – שֶׁתְּחִילַּת עֲשִׂיָּיתוֹ לְנֵזֶק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the pit's side of the pair named in Step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בור is a source of damage from its creation, and the owner stays liable even after handing it to a חרש שוטה וקטן. This is not so with אש.

steps.title: How fire is stricter than the pit
steps.stepSummary: אש moves and spreads damage, and it is מועד to consume both things fit for burning and things that are not. A בור has neither feature.
steps.simpleTranslation: How is fire stricter than a pit? Fire's way is to travel and cause damage. It is also considered forewarned to consume both things fit for it and things not fit for it. This is not so with a pit.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes the fire-and-pit pair by giving two ways fire is stricter than a pit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A pit stays in one place and only harms what comes to it. Fire travels outward to reach things and damage them. Fire is also held liable for consuming even things that are not normally its 'food'. A pit has no matching feature.

keyTerms.meaning: Its way is to go and do damage
Something fit for it, meaning something fire normally burns

phrases.english: The stringency in Fire over Pit:
that fire's way is to go and do damage,
and it is forewarned to consume
both something fit for it,
and something not fit for it;
which is not so with a pit.

steps.triggerLanguage: חוֹמֶר בְּאֵשׁ מִבְּבוֹר – שֶׁהָאֵשׁ דַּרְכָּהּ לֵילֵךְ וּלְהַזִּיק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the fire-and-pit comparison by giving fire's side.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אש travels to cause damage and is מועד for both fitting and unfitting objects. בור is not.
steps.whatToRemember: A בור is stricter because it is made in a harmful way from the start, and the owner stays liable after handing it over. אש is stricter because it moves out to do damage and consumes even things not normally fit for it.

steps.title: Why not list that an ox is liable for vessels and a pit is not?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא did not add a stringency of שור over בור: a שור is liable for damaging כלים, and a בור is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let the ברייתא also teach that an ox is stricter than a pit, because the owner of an ox pays for broken vessels, which is not so with a pit!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא for leaving out an obvious difference between שור and בור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By the usual view, a בור makes its owner pay for people and animals that fall in, but not for כלים. A שור makes its owner pay for כלים too. So this looks like a clear חומר בשור that the ברייתא should have listed.

keyTerms.meaning: A stringency, a way one case is stricter than another
Vessels or objects
But let it teach (a challenge: why was this left out?)

phrases.english: But let it also teach: a stringency of Ox over Pit
that with an ox, one is liable for vessels
which is not so with a pit!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלִיתְנֵי חוֹמֶר בְּשׁוֹר מִבְּבוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how complete the ברייתא's list of stringencies is.
steps.kashyaTarget: The list of stringencies in the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: There is a clear difference between שור and בור regarding כלים, yet the ברייתא does not list it.

steps.title: The ברייתא follows רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא follows רבי יהודה, who holds a בור liable for כלים too, so there is no difference to list.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view is this ברייתא? It is רבי יהודה, who makes a person liable for vessels damaged in his pit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא follows רבי יהודה, and by his view שור and בור are the same regarding כלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a בור also makes its owner pay for כלים, then שור is not stricter than בור on this point. So the ברייתא had nothing to list.

keyTerms.meaning: Whose view is this?
The תנא who holds a בור liable for כלים
Damage to vessels

phrases.english: Whose view is this?
It is Rabbi Yehuda
who holds one liable for damage to vessels in a pit.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא מַנִּי רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 7 by naming the author of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributing the ברייתא to a specific תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We assumed the ברייתא follows the usual view that a בור is not liable for כלים.
steps.terutzMaskana: It follows רבי יהודה, so there is no difference between שור and בור regarding כלים.

steps.title: The סיפא says a pit is not liable for vessels
steps.stepSummary: The סיפא of the ברייתא says fire is stricter than בור because fire consumes כלים, which a בור does not, so it cannot follow רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it is רבי יהודה, look at the end: fire is stricter than a pit because fire travels and damages, and is מועד to burn both what fits it and what does not, which is not so with a pit. What fits it? Wood. What does not fit it? Vessels. And it says this is not so with a pit. But if it is רבי יהודה, didn't you say he holds a pit liable for vessels?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer: the סיפא of the same ברייתא clearly says a בור is not liable for כלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא explains that the סיפא's phrase 'something not fit for fire' means כלים, and the סיפא says this is 'not so with a pit'. That means a בור does not make its owner pay for כלים, which is the opposite of רבי יהודה's view. So the ברייתא cannot follow רבי יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: Look at the latter clause
Fit for it (things that normally burn)
Wood
Considered forewarned, always liable

steps.confusionAlert: This סיפא is the same line from step 6. The גמרא is not starting a new topic; it is using that line as proof against רבי יהודה.

phrases.english: If it is Rabbi Yehuda, look at the latter clause:
A stringency of Fire over Pit
that fire's way is to travel and damage,
and it is forewarned to consume
phrases.notes: The letter in square brackets is added in the corrected wording, making the word read מוּעֶדֶת.

phrases.english: both something fit for it
and something not fit for it,
which is not so with a pit.
"Something fit for it" — what is that? Wood;

phrases.aramaic: ״דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין רָאוּי לָהּ״ מַאי נִינְהוּ – כֵּלִים;
phrases.english: "Something not fit for it" — what is that? Vessels;
and it says: "which is not so with a pit."
If it is Rabbi Yehuda —

phrases.aramaic: הָא אָמְרַתְּ מְחַיֵּיב הָיָה רַבִּי יְהוּדָה
phrases.english: didn't you say Rabbi Yehuda holds one liable
for damage to vessels in a pit!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי רַבִּי יְהוּדָה, אֵימָא סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects step 8's answer by using the ברייתא's own סיפא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the ברייתא follows רבי יהודה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The סיפא says a בור is not liable for כלים, which contradicts רבי יהודה.

steps.title: It follows the רבנן, and the תנא left some cases out
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא really follows the רבנן; the תנא listed some cases and left others out.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it really follows the רבנן, and the תנא taught some cases and left some out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the רבי יהודה answer and gives a new one: the ברייתא simply did not list every difference.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By the רבנן, the שור-over-בור point about כלים is true. It is missing only because the תנא did not try to list everything. This is the rule of תנא ושייר.

keyTerms.meaning: Actually, really
The Sages, the majority view
The תנא taught some cases and left others out

phrases.english: Rather, it really is the Rabbis,
and he taught some and left some out.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לְעוֹלָם רַבָּנַן הִיא וּתְנָא וְשַׁיַּיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected answer of step 8 with a new answer to step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: תנא ושייר — the list is not complete
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא must follow רבי יהודה to explain the missing case.
steps.terutzMaskana: It follows the רבנן; the missing case was just not listed.

steps.title: What else did he leave out?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what other case the תנא left out, which would show he also left this one out.
steps.simpleTranslation: What else did he leave out, that we can say he left this out too?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a second missing case, to back up the claim that the תנא left things out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא's rule is that you can only say תנא ושייר if at least one more case is missing. One missing case alone is not enough.

keyTerms.meaning: What did he leave out?
That this, too, was left out

phrases.english: What else did he leave out, that he left out this?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי שַׁיַּיר דְּהַאי שַׁיַּיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the answer of step 10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Another case missing from the ברייתא

steps.title: He left out hidden items
steps.stepSummary: The תנא also left out טמון, a hidden item, which fire does not make its owner pay for.
steps.simpleTranslation: He left out a hidden item.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא names the second missing case: טמון, hidden items.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Other damagers make their owner pay even for hidden things, but fire does not. That is a way other damagers are stricter than fire, and the ברייתא did not list it. So we see the תנא did leave things out.

keyTerms.meaning: A hidden or covered item
He left out
Fire, one of the main damagers

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא follows the רבנן, so a בור is not liable for כלים. The point about שור and כלים, and the point about טמון, are both missing because of תנא ושייר.

phrases.english: He left out a hidden item.
phrases.notes: A person who lit a fire does not pay for things hidden out of sight that it burned, so this is a leniency in fire that the ברייתא did not list.

steps.triggerLanguage: שַׁיַּיר טָמוּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 11 and backs up the תנא ושייר answer.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The case of טמון, which fire is not liable for, was also left out.

steps.title: Another way to read the ברייתא as רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא can still follow רבי יהודה. The phrase 'something not fitting for it' does not mean כלים. It means fire scorching a plowed field or singeing stones.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say: really it is רבי יהודה. 'Something not fitting for it' does not come to include כלים. Rather, it comes to include where the fire scorched his plowed field and singed his stones.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the idea that the ברייתא follows רבי יהודה. It solves the problem from Step 9 by reading the fire clause differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 9's problem was that the ברייתא seemed to say fire is stricter because it damages כלים, and רבי יהודה holds a בור liable for כלים too. Now the גמרא says that phrase means damage only fire can do, like scorching a plowed field or singeing stones. A pit cannot do that, so the difference stands even according to רבי יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: If you wish, say; it introduces a second, alternative answer
To include; to bring in an extra case
His plowed field
It singed or scorched lightly

phrases.english: If you wish, say:
Actually, it follows Rabbi Yehuda,
and 'something that is not fitting for it'
phrases.notes: This quotes the fire clause of the ברייתא, which was the problem in Step 9.

phrases.english: does not come to include vessels,
rather it comes to include
where it scorched his plowed field and singed his stones.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: לְעוֹלָם רַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to the קשיא of Step 9, alongside the answer of Steps 10-12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the phrase in the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Something not fitting for it' meant כלים, which would clash with רבי יהודה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The phrase means scorching a field or singeing stones, so the ברייתא fits רבי יהודה.

steps.title: רב אשי: the ברייתא should have listed פסולי המוקדשין
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי objects. Another difference between ox and בור should have been taught: an ox is liable for damaging an animal of פסולי המוקדשין, but a בור is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי objects: Let it teach that ox is stricter than pit. With an ox, one is liable for damaging an ox of פסולי המוקדשין, which is not so with a pit!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי challenges the idea that the ברייתא follows רבי יהודה. He points to a difference between ox and בור that the ברייתא never mentions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lists differences between the damagers. רב אשי notes one that is missing: an ox pays for hurting a disqualified consecrated animal, but a pit does not. A full list should have included it. The next step explains why this missing case is a problem only for רבי יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: He objects to it; he raises a strong challenge
A stringency; a way one case is stricter than another
Consecrated animals that became unfit for an offering and were redeemed
Let it teach; it should have said

phrases.english: Rav Ashi objects to this:
Let it teach a stringency of Ox over Pit:
that with Ox, one is liable
for an ox that is a disqualified consecrated animal,
phrases.notes: This is an animal set aside as a קרבן that became unfit and was redeemed. It still keeps some holiness.

phrases.english: which is not so with Pit!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the claim of Step 13 that the ברייתא follows רבי יהודה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the ברייתא follows רבי יהודה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא leaves out a real difference between ox and בור. That gap needs an explanation.

steps.title: Why the missing case is a problem only for רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: Under the רבנן, the תנא skipped כלים, so skipping פסולי המוקדשין too is easy to understand. Under רבי יהודה, what else did he skip?
steps.simpleTranslation: Granted, if you say it follows the רבנן: since he left out that case, he also left out this one. But if you say it follows רבי יהודה, what else did he leave out that would explain leaving out this?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי spells out his challenge. A missing case is acceptable only if the תנא clearly skipped other cases too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the רבנן, the תנא already left out כלים, which a בור does not pay for. That shows he wasn't listing everything, as Steps 10-12 said. Under רבי יהודה, a בור pays for כלים, so that omission disappears. Then we need another skipped case to explain why פסולי המוקדשין is missing.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted; this works fine
Since; because already
He left out; he omitted

steps.confusionAlert: רב אשי is not saying the ברייתא cannot follow the רבנן. His point is the reverse: the gap is easy to explain under the רבנן and hard to explain under רבי יהודה.

phrases.english: Granted, if you say it follows the Rabbis,
since he left out that case,
phrases.notes: 'That case' is כלים, which a בור does not pay for according to the רבנן.

phrases.english: he also left out this one.
But if you say it follows Rabbi Yehuda,
what did he leave out, that he left out this?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי אָמְרַתְּ בִּשְׁלָמָא רַבָּנַן הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the קשיא of Step 14 is a problem only for the רבי יהודה reading.
steps.kashyaTarget: The רבי יהודה reading of the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A missing case can be excused only if the תנא skipped other cases too. Under רבי יהודה, no other skipped case has been found.

steps.title: He also left out an ox trampling a plowed field
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the תנא also left out the case of an ox trampling someone's plowed field.
steps.simpleTranslation: He left out an ox that trampled on his plowed field.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer רב אשי. It names another case the תנא skipped.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ox can deliberately trample a field to damage it, and a pit cannot do that. If the תנא skipped this difference too, then skipping פסולי המוקדשין would be easy to understand even under רבי יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: Trampled; tread upon

phrases.english: He left out an ox that trampled on his plowed field.

steps.triggerLanguage: שַׁיַּיר דָּשׁ בְּנִירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question at the end of Step 15.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What other case did the תנא skip under the רבי יהודה reading?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: An ox trampling a plowed field.

steps.title: Trampling a field is already covered in the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The answer is rejected. Trampling a field was not really left out, because the ברייתא already says 'its way is to go and cause damage'.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it is because of trampling his plowed field, that is not an omission. For the ברייתא already teaches: 'since its way is to go and cause damage'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the answer of Step 16. That case is not truly missing from the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא already has a line saying this damager moves around and causes damage, unlike a pit that stays in place. That line covers the trampling case. So trampling is not a real omission, and רב אשי's question returns: under רבי יהודה, why is פסולי המוקדשין missing?

keyTerms.meaning: An omission; a case left out
Its way is to go and cause damage

steps.whatToRemember: The search for another skipped case under רבי יהודה fails. That leaves רב אשי's challenge standing against reading the ברייתא as רבי יהודה.

phrases.english: If it is because of trampling his plowed field,
that is not an omission,
for it already teaches:
phrases.notes: The letters in square brackets are the corrected wording.

phrases.english: 'since its way is to go and cause damage'!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי מִשּׁוּם דָּשׁ בְּנִירוֹ – לָאו שִׁיּוּרָא הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the answer given in Step 16.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The claim that trampling a plowed field is a skipped case
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא's line 'its way is to go and cause damage' already covers trampling, so it was never left out.

steps.title: New line of the משנה: making possible part of the damage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a new phrase from the משנה: 'I made possible part of its damage.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'I made possible part of its damage.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is starting a new topic by quoting a line from the משנה. This sets up the ברייתא that comes next to explain it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה teaches that if I helped make the damage possible, even partly, I am responsible. The גמרא now wants to see exactly what 'part' means in a real case.

keyTerms.meaning: I made possible / I set up (the conditions for damage)
part, some
its damage

phrases.english: I made possible part of its damage.
phrases.notes: This is a quote from the משנה. The rest of the line, quoted in the ברייתא next, says I must pay as if I made all of the damage possible.

steps.triggerLanguage: הִכְשַׁרְתִּי בְּמִקְצָת נִזְקוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the ox-and-pit discussion of steps 13-17 and opens a new line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who makes possible part of a damage is treated as responsible for it.

steps.title: The ברייתא's example: finishing a pit from nine to ten
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא explains the משנה: if one person digs a pit nine טפחים deep and another deepens it to ten, only the second person is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: 'I made possible part of its damage — I must pay for its damage as if I made all of it possible.' How so? If one person dug a pit nine deep, and another came and finished it to ten, the last one is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: A ברייתא gives a clear example of the משנה's rule. The person who finishes the pit to ten טפחים is fully liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A pit of ten טפחים is the depth that can kill. The second digger only added one טפח, yet he is treated as the one who made the whole pit, and the first digger is free. This shows that adding just 'part' can make you responsible for everything.

keyTerms.meaning: The רבנן taught (introduces a ברייתא)
I am liable / I owe
How so? (asks for an example)
one who digs a pit
he completed it

steps.whatToRemember: Pit dug to nine, finished to ten: by this ברייתא, only the last digger pays.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
I made possible part of its damage —
I am liable for paying its damage
as if I made all of its damage possible.
How so?
One who digs a pit nine deep,
phrases.notes: Nine טפחים (handbreadths). Ten טפחים is the depth at which a pit can kill.

phrases.english: and another came and completed it to ten —
the last one is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the משנה line quoted in step 18 with a concrete case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When one digs nine טפחים and another finishes to ten, only the last digger is liable.

steps.title: This ברייתא seems not to follow רבי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the ברייתא does not match רבי, who in another ברייתא says the last digger is liable for death, but both diggers share liability for injuries.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is not like רבי, as it was taught: If one dug a pit nine deep and another came and finished it to ten, the last one is liable. רבי says: For death, we go after the last one; for injuries, we go after both of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notes that our ברייתא seems to disagree with רבי. It brings another ברייתא where רבי splits the case into death and injuries.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our ברייתא said only the last digger is liable, with no limits. רבי agrees for death, since only the tenth טפח makes the pit deadly. But for injuries, a nine-טפחים pit could already hurt, so רבי makes both diggers liable, which clashes with our ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: and this is not like רבי
as it was taught (in a ברייתא)
for death (when an animal dies)
for injuries (damage short of death)
we go after / it is blamed on

steps.confusionAlert: רבי does not argue about death. He agrees the last digger is liable for death. The argument is only about injuries.

phrases.english: And this is not like רבי —
as it was taught:
One who digs a pit nine deep,
and another came and completed it to ten —
the last one is liable.
רבי says:
For death, we go after the last one;
for injuries, we go after both of them.
phrases.notes: A nine-טפחים pit can already injure, so both diggers had a part in the injury.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּדְלָא כְּרַבִּי – דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the ברייתא of step 19 against רבי's view.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא in step 19 that makes only the last digger liable.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי holds both diggers are liable for injuries, so a ruling that only the last is liable in every case seems to go against רבי.

steps.title: רב פפא: the ברייתא is about death, so everyone agrees
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says the first ברייתא only speaks about death, where even רבי agrees the last digger is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: The ברייתא is talking about death, and then it is everyone's opinion.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the problem from step 20. He reads our ברייתא as speaking only about an animal that died in the pit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once our ברייתא is limited to death, it matches רבי, who also blames only the last digger for death. So there is no argument, and the ברייתא follows everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: an אמורא who offers the answer
and it is everyone's opinion

steps.whatToRemember: רב פפא: our ברייתא is about death, so it matches both the תנא קמא and רבי.

phrases.english: רב פפא said:
For death, and it is everyone's opinion.
phrases.notes: He means the first ברייתא is only talking about death, which even רבי agrees with.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא אָמַר: לְמִיתָה, וְדִבְרֵי הַכֹּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the difficulty raised in step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (the ברייתא speaks only about death)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to make the last digger liable for both death and injuries, going against רבי.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about death only, where רבי agrees, so it is the view of everyone.

steps.title: Second version: Does the ברייתא disagree with רבי?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings another version of the earlier discussion. Here the problem is asked as a question: shall we say the ברייתא does not follow רבי?
steps.simpleTranslation: There are those who say the discussion went like this: Shall we say that the ברייתא is not according to רבי?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of the same discussion from steps 20 and 21, this time asking the problem as a question. This sets up רב פפא's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The content of the problem is the same as before. The ברייתא says only the last digger is liable, while רבי holds both diggers share liability for injuries. Only the way the problem is worded is different.

keyTerms.meaning: There are those who say (another version of the discussion)
Shall we say? (introduces a suggestion the גמרא will test)
רבי יהודה הנשיא, who compiled the משנה

phrases.english: There are those who say:
Shall we say it is not according to רבי?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְאָמְרִי: לֵימָא דְּלָא כְּרַבִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second version of the problem raised in step 20
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא that says only the last digger (from nine to ten טפחים) is liable
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי holds that both diggers share liability for injuries, so a ruling that only the last digger is liable seems to go against him.

steps.title: רב פפא: The ברייתא speaks about death, and everyone agrees
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that the ברייתא is talking about an animal that died in the pit. In that case everyone, including רבי, agrees that only the last digger is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: The ברייתא is about death, and in that case it is the opinion of everyone.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the question by limiting the ברייתא to cases of death. That way it does not disagree with רבי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי only splits liability between the diggers for injuries. For death, he agrees the last digger is fully liable. So the ברייתא matches all opinions.

keyTerms.meaning: Death (an animal killed by falling into the pit)
Everyone agrees

steps.whatToRemember: In both versions, רב פפא says the ברייתא about the nine-to-ten טפחים pit speaks about death, where even רבי agrees only the last digger pays.

phrases.english: רב פפא said:
It is about death, and it is the opinion of everyone.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: לְמִיתָה, וְדִבְרֵי הַכֹּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 22
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to cover injuries too, which would go against רבי.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is only about death, where everyone, including רבי, agrees only the last digger is liable.

steps.title: רבי זירא: What about the ox given to five guards?
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא asks why the ברייתא gave only the pit as an example of 'making part of the damage possible'. He suggests another case: an ox given to five people to guard, where one was careless and the ox caused damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא challenged it: Are there no other cases? But there is this case: a person gave his ox to five people to guard, one of them was careless, and the ox caused damage. That person is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא challenges the ברייתא for listing only one case. He offers the case of the five guards as another example of the משנה's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The careless guard was only one of five, so it seems he made only part of the damage possible, yet he is liable. That looks like a perfect example of the משנה's phrase, so why didn't the ברייתא mention it?

keyTerms.meaning: He challenged it (a strong objection)
And is there nothing more?
He handed over (gave to someone to guard)
He was careless (was negligent in guarding)

phrases.english: רבי זירא challenged it:
And is there nothing more?
phrases.notes: He means: is the pit really the only case of 'making part of the damage possible'?

phrases.english: But there is:
He gave his ox to five people to guard,
and one of them was careless with it,
and it caused damage, he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לָהּ רַבִּי זֵירָא: וְתוּ לֵיכָּא? וְהָא אִיכָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the ברייתא's explanation of the משנה's phrase and challenges it for being incomplete
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא that explains 'I made possible part of its damage' using only the pit case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The careless guard seems to make only part of the damage possible and is still liable, so the ברייתא should have listed this case too.

steps.title: If the ox needed all five guards, the careless one did all the damage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the case is. If the ox could not be guarded without this guard, then obviously he alone caused the damage, so this is not a case of 'part of the damage'.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If you say that without him the ox would not have been guarded, it is obvious that he caused the damage!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts to push back on רבי זירא by asking for the exact case. It tests the first possibility and shows it does not fit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If all five were needed, the one careless guard is what let the ox go free. Then he caused the whole damage, not part of it. So this case is no example of the משנה's phrase.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? (how exactly does it look?)
If you say (introduces the first possibility)
Guarded
It is obvious

phrases.english: What is the case?
If you say that without him
it would not have been guarded,
it is obvious that he is the one who caused it!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָמֵי? אִילֵּימָא דִּבְלָאו אִיהוּ לָא הֲוָה מִינְּטַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins rejecting רבי זירא's suggested case
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The first way of picturing the five-guard case
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: If the guard was needed, he caused all the damage, so it is not 'part of the damage'.

steps.title: If the ox was guarded anyway, the careless one did nothing
steps.stepSummary: The other possibility is that the ox was safely guarded even without him. But then he did nothing to cause the damage, so this case does not fit either.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the case is where even without him it would have been guarded? Then what did he do?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the second possibility and shows it fails too. This finishes the rejection of רבי זירא's challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the other four were enough, his carelessness changed nothing. So he did not make even part of the damage possible. Either way, the five-guard case is not an example of the משנה's phrase, which is why the ברייתא left it out.

keyTerms.meaning: Without him
What did he do? (he did nothing)

steps.whatToRemember: The five-guard case does not fit 'part of the damage': either the careless guard caused all of it, or he caused none of it.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the גמרא is asking whether the careless guard pays. It is only showing that his case does not fit the משנה's phrase 'part of the damage'.

phrases.english: Rather, where even without him it would have been guarded?
What did he do?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא דִּבְלָאו אִיהוּ נָמֵי מִינְּטַר? מַאי קָעָבֵיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the two-sided rejection begun in step 25
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: רבי זירא's whole challenge from the five-guard case
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: If he was not needed, he caused nothing at all, so the case never shows 'part of the damage'.

steps.title: רב ששת: What about adding a bundle of wood to a fire?
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת offers another case the ברייתא could have listed: someone who makes a fire bigger by adding a bundle of wood.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת challenged it: But there is the case of one who adds a bundle to a fire!
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת raises a new challenge to the ברייתא for listing only the pit. He suggests a person who adds wood to a fire as another example.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fire was already there, and he only made it stronger. That seems to be making part of the damage possible, so the ברייתא should have mentioned this case.

keyTerms.meaning: Adds to, makes bigger
A bundle (of wood or branches)

phrases.english: רב ששת challenged it:
But there is the one who adds a bundle!
phrases.notes: He means someone who adds a bundle of wood to a fire that is already burning, making it bigger.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לָהּ רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: וְהָא אִיכָּא מַרְבֶּה בַּחֲבִילָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge of the same kind as רבי זירא's, using a new case
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא that lists only the pit case for 'I made possible part of its damage'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Adding a bundle to an existing fire only increases damage that was already possible, so it seems to be another example that the ברייתא left out.

steps.title: What exactly is the case of the added bundle?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the exact details of רב ששת's case of adding a bundle of wood to a fire. This opens the way to show why the case may not fit.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are the circumstances?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the case of adding wood to a fire looks like. This is a setup line: it is preparing to look at the possible versions of the case one at a time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ששת said the ברייתא could have listed someone who adds a bundle of wood to a fire. Before accepting this, the גמרא wants to pin down exactly what happened. This is the same pattern it used with the ox and the five guards in steps 25 and 26. There, it found that in each possible version, the person either caused the whole damage or caused none of it.

keyTerms.meaning: What are the circumstances? What exactly is the case?
How? In what way?
Is it like, does it look like (from the word for 'similar')

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not the answer yet. It is only the opening question, and the actual testing of the case continues on the next amud.

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to רב ששת's suggested case from step 27 by asking for its exact details. This follows the same pattern used against רבי זירא's case in step 25.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact situation of a person who adds a bundle of wood to a fire, so the גמרא can test whether he really caused only part of the damage.
